title: Diabetic neuropathic foot ulcer: sensory impairment
vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of a foot wound. The patient noticed a small ulcer on the bottom of his right foot a week ago but recalls no significant foot injury. He has been applying antiseptics, but the wound has failed to heal. The patient has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and is nonadherent to medical therapy. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 72/min. Right lower extremity examination shows a 1-cm (0.39-in) plantar ulcer under the first metatarsal head. There are no other lesions, and the tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are normal. Which of the following is the strongest contributing factor underlying the development of this patient's foot ulcer?

clues.note: An ulcer developing without a remembered injury implies the patient did not FEEL the causative trauma/pressure - a clue to sensory neuropathy.

clues.text: 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and is nonadherent to medical therapy
clues.note: Long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes causes peripheral sensory neuropathy - the key risk factor for neuropathic foot ulcers.

clues.text: plantar ulcer under the first metatarsal head
clues.note: Ulcers over weight-bearing bony prominences (e.g., first metatarsal head) are classic neuropathic (pressure) ulcers.

clues.text: tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are normal
clues.note: Intact distal pulses argue AGAINST arterial insufficiency as the cause, supporting a neuropathic (not ischemic) ulcer.

whatMatters: A PAINLESS plantar ulcer over a weight-bearing bony prominence (first metatarsal head) in long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes with NORMAL pulses = a NEUROPATHIC ulcer. The strongest underlying factor is SENSORY IMPAIRMENT (diabetic peripheral neuropathy): loss of protective sensation lets repetitive pressure/trauma go unnoticed. Answer D.
strategy: Distinguish ulcer types: NEUROPATHIC (painless, over pressure points/plantar, normal pulses, from sensory loss) vs ARTERIAL (painful, at toes/lateral malleolus, decreased pulses) vs VENOUS (medial malleolus, irregular, stasis changes). Normal pulses + painless plantar ulcer = neuropathic -> sensory impairment. Reject atherosclerotic/arterial (pulses normal), bacterial infection (a complication, not the inciting cause), irritant dermatitis (no ulcers), vasculitis (painful, systemic), and venous insufficiency (medial malleolus/varicosities).

eliminations.label: Atherosclerotic disease - arterial ulcers are painful, pulses decreased
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: peripheral arterial disease causing ischemic ulcers. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: arterial ulcers are PAINFUL, sharply demarcated, at the toe TIPS, with DECREASED/absent pulses; this patient has normal pulses and a painless plantar ulcer. ✅ Correct if: painful toe-tip ulcer with diminished pulses (PAD).

eliminations.label: Bacterial infection - a complication, not the cause
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: secondary infection that can delay healing. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: infection may complicate a neuropathic ulcer but is not the INCITING cause; there's no fever, erythema, or purulence here. ✅ Correct if: osteomyelitis/cellulitis complicating the wound.

eliminations.label: Irritant dermatitis - causes rash, not ulcers
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: skin irritation from contact exposure (pruritic/painful erythema, sometimes fissures). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it typically affects exposed skin and doesn't produce a plantar pressure ulcer. ✅ Correct if: an eczematous contact reaction on exposed skin.

eliminations.label: Systemic vasculitis - uncommon, painful, systemic
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: vasculitic skin ulcers (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these are usually painful and accompanied by systemic/other skin findings (purpura, nodules), not an isolated painless plantar pressure ulcer. ✅ Correct if: ulcers with systemic vasculitic features.

eliminations.label: Venous insufficiency - medial malleolus, not plantar
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: venous stasis ulcers. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they occur over the MEDIAL malleolus with stasis dermatitis/varicosities and hyperpigmentation, not under the first metatarsal head. ✅ Correct if: irregular medial-ankle ulcer with venous stasis changes.

reasoning: Painless plantar ulcer over a weight-bearing bony prominence, no remembered injury
Long-standing poorly controlled diabetes causes sensory peripheral neuropathy
Loss of protective sensation lets repetitive pressure/trauma cause a nonhealing ulcer
Normal pulses exclude arterial disease -> the cause is sensory impairment; answer D
mechanism: Chronic hyperglycemia damages peripheral nerves and impairs their repair, producing a length-dependent DISTAL SENSORY (and autonomic/motor) neuropathy. Loss of PROTECTIVE SENSATION (pain, pressure, proprioception) means the patient does not perceive minor trauma, friction, or sustained pressure - especially over weight-bearing bones such as the plantar surface of the FIRST METATARSAL HEAD - so repetitive injury goes unnoticed and progresses to a nonhealing NEUROPATHIC ulcer. Autonomic neuropathy (dry, cracked skin) and motor neuropathy with foot deformities (Charcot foot, hammertoes shifting pressure points) contribute further. Because distal PULSES are NORMAL here, arterial insufficiency is not the primary driver (though many diabetics also have peripheral arterial disease). Management centers on PRESSURE OFFLOADING, glycemic control, wound care, and infection surveillance. The other options are either different ulcer types (arterial, venous), complications rather than causes (bacterial infection), or unrelated (irritant dermatitis, vasculitis).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Endo/Neuro > diabetic neuropathic foot ulcer: sensory neuropathy -> painless plantar ulcer over pressure points; normal pulses; offloading. Contrast arterial (painful, toe tips, ↓pulses) and venous (medial malleolus) ulcers.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Painless plantar ulcer + normal pulses + long-standing diabetes = neuropathic ulcer (sensory impairment).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on neuropathic vs arterial vs venous ulcer, protective sensation, Charcot foot, or offloading? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Arterial (pulses normal here), infection (complication), vasculitis (painful/systemic), venous (medial malleolus), dermatitis (rash) don't fit.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: diabetic neuropathic ulcer = sensory loss -> painless plantar pressure ulcer, normal pulses; treat with offloading + glycemic control.

keywords.front: Painless plantar ulcer over a bony prominence in a diabetic

keywords.back: Arterial: painful, toe tips, ↓pulses; neuropathic: painless, plantar, normal pulses
Pressure offloading + glycemic control + wound care
Loss of protective sensation (diabetic peripheral neuropathy)

firstAid.detail: Endo: sensory neuropathy -> painless plantar pressure ulcer; normal pulses; offloading.
Vasc > arterial (painful/toe tips), venous (medial malleolus), neuropathic (plantar).

memoryHook: Numb feet don't complain: a diabetic can't feel the pressure grinding under the first metatarsal, so a painless ulcer bores in while the pulses stay strong.
